conflict_topics: use of shared kitchen and scheduling
dialogue_quality_notes: Pragmatic, solution-oriented negotiation: proposals with clear trade-offs (timing, frequency, ventilation, scheduling).
Multiple concrete proposals were tested (after 7pm, open window, once-a-week cooking, specific days) and countered with factual constraints (service yard proximity, laundry days).
Several near-duplicate confirmations after settlement ('Okay, that works for me.') produced mild repetitiveness across rounds 10–12.
evaluation.final_reason: Parties reached a concrete compromise: Agent D agreed to change cooking behavior (reduced frequency and timing) in response to others' requests. Key lines: 'Okay, after 7 is fine for me.' (Agent D agreeing to A's timing), 'Okay, once a week is fine.' (Agent D accepting reduced frequency), 'I'll cook on a Tuesday or Thursday then.' (Agent D offering days to avoid C's laundry), and 'Okay, that works for me.' (Agent C accepting). In short, D conceded to cook only once a week, after 7pm, on a Tuesday or Thursday; others accepted that arrangement.
position_change_notes: Agent D moved from an initial defensive stance ('this is the only kitchen, and we all have to cook') to accepting constraints: 'Okay, after 7 is fine for me.' and 'Okay, once a week is fine.' and 'I'll cook on a Tuesday or Thursday then.'
Agent A moved from requesting a ban on strong-smelling food to accepting a time-limited accommodation ('That works for me.' in response to after-7pm).
Agents B and C consistently raised affected interests (room smell, laundry) and ultimately accepted the frequency/day compromise; C explicitly accepted the proposed days ('Okay, that works for me.').

round_scores.evidence: Agent A reports a work impact: 'The smell is a problem for my work. I'm on video calls...' and Agent B reports personal impact: 'It gets into my room too.' A request (no strong-smelling food) is pending; grievances are voiced but no opposing position yet.

Agent C: 'My laundry... all smells like curry now.' Agent D responds with the core opposing practical claim: 'Okay, I hear you. But this is the only kitchen, and we all have to cook.' This expresses a clear, entrenched incompatibility between D's need/use and others' requests.

Agent A proposes a modification to accommodate work: 'My calls are done by 7 p.m. Could you cook it after then?' Agent D accepts that timing: 'Okay, after 7 is fine for me.' The disagreement softens but the laundry/smell issue remains ('that doesn't help with the smell on your clothes, right?').

Agent A: 'That works for me.' But Agent B resists on the ground of persistent smell: 'But that doesn't change the smell. It will still get into my room.' The earlier partial agreement is challenged, re-elevating the incompatibility.

Agent C: 'Same for me... my laundry still gets the smell overnight.' Agent D: 'Right. So what's the solution then? I can't change the kitchen.' The parties restate positions and the practical constraint, leaving the conflict unresolved.

Agent B proposes ventilation: 'Can we open the kitchen window when cooking? If we all keep our doors closed, it should help.' Agent C counters the practical effect on laundry: 'The service yard is right next to the kitchen. The smell will go straight to the laundry anyway.' Proposal met with factual counter, conflict persists.

Agent D asks for workable options ('Is there anything that *does* work, besides me not cooking?') and Agent B offers a concrete compromise: 'How about cooking a larger portion once a week instead of twice?' This moves toward reducing the frequency of the nuisance.

Agent D accepts the frequency compromise: 'Okay, once a week is fine.' Agent B: 'Okay, that works for me.' The core behavioral change is agreed in principle, though scheduling and laundry-day conflicts remain unsettled.

Agent C raises scheduling constraints: 'Which day? I do my laundry on Mondays, Wednesdays, and Fridays.' Agent D offers specific alternative days to avoid those: 'I'll cook on a Tuesday or Thursday then.' The parties narrow the outstanding issue (schedule).

Agent C accepts the proposed schedule: 'Okay, that works for me.' Combined with earlier acceptances (D: 'Okay, once a week is fine.'; D: 'Okay, after 7 is fine for me.'), the remaining substantive incompatibility (frequency and day) is settled.
Rounds contain repeated confirmations ('Okay, that works for me.' by Agent C) after the settlement in round 10; no new substantive disagreement appears.
Further repetitions of acceptance only; no new substantive issues raised.

substantive_insights: Conflict centered on incompatible practical uses of a single shared kitchen: D's cooking frequency vs others' need for smoke-free workspace and clean laundry.
Physical constraints (landlord forbids kitchen changes; service yard next to kitchen) limited ventilation solutions, steering parties toward behavioral compromises (frequency and scheduling).
A layered compromise (timing to protect A's calls, reduced frequency to limit overall exposure, and scheduling to avoid C's laundry days) resolved the multi-party incompatibility.
